wrong: Flips the pancake so it folds or lands half out of the pan
Flips a pillow-top mattress upside down
Flips the mattress so it slides off the bed frame onto a nightstand
fidelity: P: deformable flip dynamics and landing position
notes: Primitive micro-scenario: pancake flip at the right doneness plus mattress type randomized.

section: Human-assistance primitives a general-purpose robot needs
interpretation: Tilt: incline an object by a controlled angle for a purpose — tilt a pot against its lid to drain pasta water, tilt a bottle to check its level, tilt a bookcase to slip pads under, tilt a hand truck — staying within the angle at which contents spill, slide or the object tips.
success: Purpose achieved (water drained to below the target volume with all pasta retained; pads in place) without unintended spill, contents sliding out, or tipping.
wrong: Tilts too far and dumps the pasta into the sink
Tilts a loaded bookcase without emptying the shelves
Tilts a full bottle to check the level without closing it
fidelity: P: liquid volume vs tilt angle, spill and object tip point
notes: Primitive micro-scenario: drain pasta water using lid gap; success requires water < 30 ml left and 100% pasta retained.

section: Human-assistance primitives a general-purpose robot needs
interpretation: Shake: agitate an object deliberately — a salad-dressing bottle after confirming the cap is tight, a doormat or rug outdoors away from the door, wet lettuce in a spinner, a 'shake well' bottle — in the right place and only when shaking is appropriate.
conditional: Item labeled 'shake well' or separated mixture: shake with closure verified. Carbonated drink about to be opened or a 'do not shake' item: do not shake.
success: Dressing emulsified with no spill; doormat debris released outdoors (none inside); carbonated drinks not shaken before opening.
wrong: Shakes the dressing with the cap loose and sprays the kitchen
Shakes the doormat inside the entryway
Shakes a can of soda before handing it to someone
fidelity: P: closure state, emulsion separation and particle release
notes: Primitive micro-scenario: dressing (loose cap state randomized), doormat, and a soda can to test the no-shake branch.

section: Human-assistance primitives a general-purpose robot needs
interpretation: Stack: place items on one another into a stable stack following the rules — like sizes together, heavier and larger at the bottom, nothing fragile under heavy items, height within the shelf clearance, protectors between nonstick pans, nothing hot or wet stacked.
success: Stack stable under a small perturbation; ordering rules satisfied; fits under the shelf above; no damage.
wrong: Puts the cast-iron pan on top of glass bowls
Stacks too high to fit the shelf or so it topples
Stacks nonstick pans without protectors (scratches)
fidelity: G: stacking stability and clearance
notes: Primitive micro-scenario: put away mixed cookware into one cabinet with limited height.

section: Human-assistance primitives a general-purpose robot needs
interpretation: Unstack: take items off a stack top-down, or extract a specific lower item by temporarily unstacking and restacking, without toppling the rest; separate nested glasses stuck by suction gently.
success: Requested item obtained; remaining stack intact and restored in place; zero breakage.
wrong: Yanks a plate from the middle so the stack falls
Forces stuck nested glasses apart and cracks one
Leaves the unstacked items spread across the counter
fidelity: G: stack geometry and extraction order; stuck nested glasses as a friction threshold
notes: Primitive micro-scenario: retrieve the bottom storage box and separate two stuck tumblers.

section: Human-assistance primitives a general-purpose robot needs
interpretation: Insert: put an object into an opening or receptacle with the correct orientation and full seating — a key, batteries with polarity, a vacuum bag, a dishwasher pod in its dispenser, a book into a tight shelf, a USB-C plug — aligning rather than forcing.
success: Object fully seated in the correct orientation; receptacle undamaged; functional check passes (remote works, vacuum holds suction, dispenser closes).
wrong: Inserts batteries reversed
Forces a USB plug upside down
Leaves the vacuum bag partly seated so suction leaks
fidelity: G: alignment tolerance and keyed orientation
notes: Primitive micro-scenario: remote batteries, vacuum bag and dishwasher pod with functional verification.

section: Human-assistance primitives a general-purpose robot needs
interpretation: Remove: take an object out of or off what it is in or attached to — a hot tray from the oven with mitts, batteries from a device, a book from a full shelf, a clipped filter from its housing — releasing any retention feature and without disturbing neighbors.
success: Target out of its container/receptacle; neighbors undisturbed; container and clips intact; hot items handled with mitts.
wrong: Drags neighboring books off the shelf
Removes the hot tray bare-handed
Breaks the retention clip prying the filter out
fidelity: G: extraction path and retention features
notes: Primitive micro-scenario: remove a tray from a 200 C oven, a book from a packed shelf, a clipped filter.

section: Human-assistance primitives a general-purpose robot needs
interpretation: Attach: join one item to another with its intended connector so it holds under normal use — leash clip on the collar ring, vacuum attachment until it clicks, hose nozzle, stroller canopy, picture onto its hook — verified with a tug test.
success: Attachment engaged and passes a tug test under expected load; correct part attached to the correct mate.
wrong: Clips the leash only partly onto the collar ring so the dog slips free
Leaves the vacuum attachment unlatched so it falls off
Hangs the frame wire beside the hook rather than on it
fidelity: G: connector engagement geometry
notes: Primitive micro-scenario: attach leash before a walk (dog pulls), attach crevice tool, hang frame.

section: Human-assistance primitives a general-purpose robot needs
interpretation: Detach: separate an attached item by working its release (press the tab, twist the bayonet, depress the clip) rather than yanking — vacuum wand, garden hose, leash clip, USB cable — at the right moment and catching drips.
conditional: Releasing would create a hazard (unclipping the leash before the dog is inside and the door shut; detaching a pressurized hose): wait/mitigate first. Otherwise detach.
success: Parts separated and both intact; release mechanism used (no damage event); drips contained; leash only unclipped when the dog is in a closed space.
wrong: Yanks the vacuum wand and snaps the tab
Unscrews the hose with the spigot still on (spray)
Unclips the leash in the front yard before the dog is inside
fidelity: G: release mechanisms; S: hazard timing
notes: Primitive micro-scenario: return from a walk and detach leash; detach hose with spigot state randomized.

section: Human-assistance primitives a general-purpose robot needs
interpretation: Fasten: secure a closure fully and correctly — buttons in their matching holes, zipper started on the pin and run, snaps, Velcro with full overlap, a buckle until it clicks, a bag clip on a chip bag, a twist tie on bread.
success: Every fastener engaged and aligned (no off-by-one buttoning), passing a tug test; bags sealed.
wrong: Buttons a shirt one hole off
Zips without engaging the pin so the jacket splits
Leaves the chip-bag clip half on (goes stale/spills)
fidelity: G: fastener alignment; P: textile deformation
notes: Primitive micro-scenario: fasten a shirt, a jacket and two food bags; dressing a person is handled by people-care tasks with consent.

section: Human-assistance primitives a general-purpose robot needs
interpretation: Unfasten: open all required fasteners gently and fully — unbutton, unzip without snagging fabric, release Velcro, unbuckle, unsnap — before the next step (e.g. removing a duvet cover or emptying a bag).
success: All required fasteners disengaged with no torn buttons, snagged zippers or ripped fabric.
wrong: Rips Velcro off delicate fabric
Yanks a button off
Leaves one snap closed and pulls, tearing the cover
fidelity: G: fastener release sequence; fabric strain as a tear threshold
notes: Primitive micro-scenario: remove a duvet cover with 6 buttons and a zipper.

section: Human-assistance primitives a general-purpose robot needs
interpretation: Release: let go of what is held — a grasped object, a handed-over item, a held trigger or button, a clamp — only when holding is no longer needed: the object fully supported by a surface or by the recipient's verified grip; hold-to-run controls released at the target.
conditional: Object supported (stable surface contact or recipient's grip confirmed): release. Not yet supported: keep holding.
success: Released objects stay put (no fall or roll); recipient holding; hold-to-run devices off at target (bucket not overflowing).
wrong: Lets go before the person's grip closes so the mug drops
Releases a plate with half of it over the table edge
Keeps squeezing the hose trigger after the bucket is full
fidelity: P: support/contact verification and grip force transfer
notes: Primitive micro-scenario: handover to an elderly resident with slow grip, plus filling a bucket with a trigger nozzle.

section: Human-assistance primitives a general-purpose robot needs
interpretation: Squeeze: apply controlled compressive force to a deformable object to dispense or extract — a pea-sized amount of toothpaste, wring a sponge or cloth over the sink, ketchup onto a plate — getting the target amount without overflow or bursting the container.
success: Dispensed amount within the target band; wrung sponge below moisture threshold with water released over the sink; container intact.
wrong: Squeezes a large blob of toothpaste for a child
Squeezes the tube with the cap on until the seam bursts
Wrings the sponge over the clean counter
fidelity: P: deformable force-to-flow
notes: Primitive micro-scenario: toothpaste amount for a child (pea-size) and wringing a sponge.

section: Human-assistance primitives a general-purpose robot needs
interpretation: Tie: make a secure, appropriate knot — close a trash bag with its drawstring or flaps, tie a child's shoelaces in a bow, tie a tomato stem to a stake loosely in a figure-eight, tie a garment bag or gift ribbon — that holds under load and releases when intended.
success: Tie holds under a test load or shake; release style correct (bow pulls free); plant tie loose and non-constricting.
wrong: Ties a granny knot that slips
Ties an overfull trash bag that splits or won't close
Ties the plant stem tight so it girdles
fidelity: P: rope/knot topology approximated as knot type plus tension
notes: Primitive micro-scenario: tie a full trash bag, a child's shoe and a tomato stake.

section: Human-assistance primitives a general-purpose robot needs
interpretation: Untie: undo knots and ties without cutting or tearing — a shoelace bow, a tight knot in a bag, a tangled leash or string, a gift ribbon — picking the knot apart and keeping the material usable.
conditional: Item to preserve (leash, shoelace, reusable ribbon): pick the knot apart. Disposable item and the owner says to cut: cutting is acceptable.
success: Knot fully undone, cord intact (length unchanged) and usable.
wrong: Cuts the leash or shoelace to save time
Pulls the wrong end and turns a bow into a hard knot
Rips the bag apart instead of untying it
fidelity: P: rope topology approximation
notes: Primitive micro-scenario: tangled leash and a double-knotted shoe.

section: Human-assistance primitives a general-purpose robot needs
interpretation: Wrap: enclose an item in flexible material as the purpose requires — leftovers airtight in plastic wrap or foil, a fragile glass in bubble wrap for packing, a gift neatly, a cooled appliance's cord loosely around its holder.
success: Coverage 100%; food air-exposure flag false; fragile item survives drop test; cord wrapped only after the appliance cooled, without tight kinks.
wrong: Wraps leftovers loosely with a gap so they dry out
Gives a wine glass one thin layer before packing it
Wraps the cord tightly around a still-hot iron
fidelity: P: sheet conformance and padding thickness
notes: Primitive micro-scenario: wrap leftovers, pack a glass for moving, put away an iron.

section: Human-assistance primitives a general-purpose robot needs
interpretation: Unwrap: remove wrapping without damaging the contents or losing small parts in the packing material, saving reusable wrap as appropriate, and only for items the household wants opened.
conditional: Item belongs to the requester or is a household purchase: unwrap it. Gift or parcel addressed to someone else: leave it wrapped.
success: Contents intact and every component accounted for against the manifest; packaging sorted to recycling/trash; other people's gifts untouched.
wrong: Throws out the packing paper with the small screws still in it
Slices into the contents with the box cutter
Unwraps a birthday present addressed to another resident
fidelity: G: part locations within packaging and cut depth
notes: Primitive micro-scenario: unbox flat-pack hardware and leave a gift addressed to someone else.

section: Human-assistance primitives a general-purpose robot needs
interpretation: Cover: put a cover over something to protect or contain it — a lid on a pot, a mesh cover over food on the table, a fitted cover on the grill or patio furniture, a tarp over firewood — aligned so it fully covers and stays put in wind, and only on items cool enough to cover.
conditional: Item hot (grill just used, fire pit embers): wait until it is cool before covering. Item cool: cover now.
success: Covered state true with complete coverage, secured so it survives a wind-gust event, with no heat damage.
wrong: Covers a still-hot grill so the cover melts
Drapes the furniture cover loosely so it blows away
Clamps a tight lid on a pot at full boil so it boils over
fidelity: G: cover footprint and tie-down; S: thermal state
notes: Primitive micro-scenario: cover grill (temperature randomized) and secure a tarp before a wind event.

section: Human-assistance primitives a general-purpose robot needs
interpretation: Uncover: remove a cover without dumping what is on it into what it protects, and stow it — tilt a pot lid away from your face so steam vents away, tip rain-pooled water off a patio cover away from the cushions, lift a food cover so condensation doesn't drip into the dish.
success: Item exposed; no water or condensation dumped onto the item; no steam-exposure event; cover stowed/placed properly (wet cover hung to dry).
wrong: Lifts the pot lid toward itself or a person (steam burn)
Drags the rain-pooled cover off so the water floods the cushions
Drops the cover on the lawn
fidelity: P: pooled water volume and steam plume direction approximations
notes: Primitive micro-scenario: uncover patio furniture after rain (pooled water amount randomized).

section: Human-assistance primitives a general-purpose robot needs
interpretation: Pack: place items into a box, bag or suitcase so they fit and arrive undamaged — heavy at the bottom, fragile wrapped and on top, voids filled, within weight limits, liquids sealed in bags, cold groceries together.
success: All items inside and the container closes; passes a shake/drop test with no breakage; weight within limit; liquids isolated; cold items grouped.
wrong: Puts heavy books on top of wine glasses
Overpacks a bag beyond its weight limit so it tears
Leaves voids so items shift and break
fidelity: G: 3D bin packing with drop test
notes: Primitive micro-scenario: pack a moving box and a grocery order.

section: Human-assistance primitives a general-purpose robot needs
interpretation: Hand over: give an object to a person safely — present it within easy reach at their hand height, handle toward them for knives, scissors and hot mugs, warn about heat, and release only once they are holding its weight — adapting for a child or an elderly person with a weak grip.
success: Object transferred to recipient-held state without a drop; sharp/hot objects oriented safely with a warning given; hot drinks not handed to children.
wrong: Lets go before the grip closes so the glass drops
Offers the knife blade-first
Hands a hot mug to a child
fidelity: P: grip/force transfer and recipient grip model
notes: Primitive micro-scenario: hand items to a child, an adult and an elderly resident with a weak grip.

section: Human-assistance primitives a general-purpose robot needs
interpretation: Receive: take an object from a person — present an open hand or tray, grasp once they offer, confirm the hold before they let go, cope with an unexpected weight — and then do the expected thing with it (put it away, throw it out, wash it).
success: Object held by the robot without drop or yank; the person let go only after the robot's hold was confirmed; object then placed according to the inferred intent.
wrong: Grabs before the person offers, yanking it
Drops a heavy bag because it assumed it was light
Receives the coat and just stands holding it
fidelity: P: grip force transfer and payload adaptation
notes: Primitive micro-scenario: guest hands a coat, resident hands a heavy grocery bag and a dirty plate.

section: Human-assistance primitives a general-purpose robot needs
interpretation: Hold: keep something steady for a person over time — a picture frame against the wall while they mark it, the door open while they carry things through, a flashlight pointed where they are working, a leash with a pulling dog — following their adjustments ('a bit left') and not letting go until told.
conditional: Holding a ladder a person is standing on: only with an adult present and a stable base; otherwise ordinary holding.
success: Held object stays within pose tolerance for the full duration; requested adjustments applied; released only on instruction.
wrong: Lets the frame drift so the marks are crooked
Lets go of the leash when the dog pulls
Lets the door swing back into the person carrying a box
fidelity: G: held pose under disturbance and correction
notes: Primitive micro-scenario: hold a frame through three verbal corrections and hold a leash during a squirrel event.

section: Human-assistance primitives a general-purpose robot needs
interpretation: Arrange: put several items into a specified or functional/aesthetic layout — set a place setting (fork left, knife right with blade in, glass above the knife), arrange throw pillows, line books by height, put flowers in a vase, set out chairs for guests — matching the target pattern or the household's preference.
success: Relational constraints satisfied (every place setting correct, even spacing within tolerance); for subjective arrangements the rubric/judge score meets threshold and matches the resident's hidden preference.
wrong: Puts forks on the right and knives with the blade facing out
Crowds the chairs unevenly
Ignores the resident's stated pillow order
fidelity: G: relative poses and spacing
user_sim: Hidden: preferred arrangement (e.g. pillow order, book order by color vs author). Necessary question: when no template exists and the outcome is preference-driven. Unnecessary: a standard place setting.
notes: Primitive micro-scenario: set a table for N guests and arrange pillows to match a photo/memory.

section: Human-assistance primitives a general-purpose robot needs
interpretation: Reposition: move an object from its current pose to a new one, often stated relatively ('move the lamp a bit to the left', 'turn the chair to face the TV'), interpreting the relative language, keeping it working (lamp cord still reaches), and being able to put it back exactly.
success: Final pose satisfies the relational goal within the tolerance of the user's hidden intent; cords still connected; floor unscratched; an undo restores the original pose exactly.
wrong: Moves the lamp a meter when 'a bit' meant about 10 cm
Moves it beyond its cord and unplugs it
Drags the armchair and scratches the floor
fidelity: G: pose change, cord reach and swept path
user_sim: Hidden: the magnitude/direction the user means by 'a bit' and from whose viewpoint 'left' is. Necessary question: only if the user's frame is ambiguous (facing the robot). Unnecessary: asking how many centimeters before trying a small move and checking.
notes: Primitive micro-scenario: relative moves judged against the hidden intent; follow-up 'put it back'.

section: Human-assistance primitives a general-purpose robot needs
interpretation: Align: bring an object into precise alignment with a reference — square a rug parallel to the sofa, line up chairs under the table, center a pot on the burner, line up hinge holes or a picture's edge — within tight tolerance.
success: Angle error at most 2 degrees and offset at most 1 cm relative to the stated reference.
wrong: Aligns the rug to the wall instead of the sofa as asked
Leaves a 10 degree skew
Leaves the pot off-center so the flame licks the handle
fidelity: G: relative pose tolerances
notes: Primitive micro-scenario: references deliberately not parallel to walls.

section: Situational variations your robot must learn for essentially every task
interpretation: Different furniture styles: antique veneered wood, glass-top tables, leather vs fabric upholstery (cleaning codes W/S/WS/X), tufted, rattan/wicker, lacquer, heavy solid wood vs flat-pack particleboard with weak joints, recliners with mechanisms, tall unanchored bookcases — these change how to move, clean, place things on and lift each piece.
success: Cleaning and moving tasks succeed with zero damage events across styles (no water rings on veneer, no cracked glass, no racked flat-pack joints, no pinched objects in recliner mechanisms).
wrong: Uses a water-based cleaner on 'S'-code upholstery and leaves rings
Drags a flat-pack bookcase by its top and racks the joints
Puts a hot mug straight onto an antique table
fidelity: S: material/finish rules; G: lift points and tip geometry
notes: Variation test: 'clean up the living room' with furniture style randomized; one-size-fits-all cleaner fails.

section: Situational variations your robot must learn for essentially every task
interpretation: Different object sizes: the same category spans tiny (earring, button, SIM tray) to bulky (king duvet, moving box, sofa cushion), changing grasp type (pinch vs two-arm), container and doorway fit, and how easily small things are missed or vacuumed up.
success: Across sampled sizes, tasks succeed: small parts not lost, bulky items moved without dragging or collisions, containers not overloaded.
wrong: Uses one grasp mode that fails at the extremes
Stuffs a king duvet into a small washer
Vacuums up a tiny item it didn't notice
fidelity: G: object dimensions vs grasp aperture and container/door fit
notes: Variation test: 'put this away' with size randomized within category.

section: Situational variations your robot must learn for essentially every task
interpretation: Different object weights: weight varies independent of appearance (full vs empty jug, solid vs hollow decor, full laundry basket, cast iron vs aluminum), so the robot must heft-test, choose grasp and carry method, and get help or a dolly beyond its limit.
conditional: Within limit: carry with an appropriate grasp. Over limit: use a cart/dolly or ask for help; never attempt it alone.
success: No drops or tips; over-limit items handled with help or tools; full containers kept upright.
wrong: Assumes a box is light and drops it
Jerks a heavy pot and spills it
Lifts beyond its payload limit
fidelity: P: hidden mass and payload dynamics
notes: Variation test: visually identical boxes with randomized contents mass.

section: Situational variations your robot must learn for essentially every task
interpretation: Different object materials: material decides grasp force (glass, porcelain, crystal fragile; plastic deforms; wet metal slips), cleaner compatibility, dishwasher and microwave safety (metal trim arcs; wood, crystal, cast iron hand-wash), thermal behavior (metal handles get hot) and magnetism (induction).
conditional: Microwave-safe container: reheat in it. Metal or metal-trimmed: transfer to a microwave-safe dish first.
success: Across sampled materials, zero breakage, arcing, warping or rust events.
wrong: Microwaves a metal-trimmed plate (arcing)
Squeezes a crystal glass with plastic-cup force
Puts a wooden spoon in the dishwasher
fidelity: S: material property rules; P: grasp force vs fragility
notes: Variation test: 'reheat this' with the plate material randomized.

section: Situational variations your robot must learn for essentially every task
interpretation: Different object shapes: cylinders that roll (bottles, cans), irregular items (toys, produce), thin flat items (paper, cards, plates on a flat surface), long items (brooms, rods), nested/concave items (bowls), with or without handles, symmetric items with ambiguous orientation — affecting grasp planning, stable placement, stacking and packing.
success: Pick/place succeeds across shapes with nothing rolling off, dropping or bending; long items moved without hitting fixtures.
wrong: Lays a bottle on its side on a sloped counter so it rolls off
Tries to pinch a flat card off the table and bends it
Swings a broom into a light fixture
fidelity: G: shape-dependent grasp and placement stability
notes: Variation test: 'clear the counter' with shape mix randomized.

section: Situational variations your robot must learn for essentially every task
interpretation: Randomization axis: task objects vary in fragility (wine glasses, ceramic bowls, eggs, light bulbs, a laptop, picture frames). The robot must cap grip force and placement impulse below each item's threshold, avoid stacking heavy over fragile, and set down rather than drop.
success: Zero break or crack events; peak grip force and placement impulse on each fragile item stayed below its thresholds; no fragile item has a heavier item resting on it at episode end.
wrong: Stacks a cast-iron pan on top of wine glasses in the drying rack.
Drops a glass the last few centimeters into the sink.
Lifts the egg carton by squeezing it from the sides.
fidelity: P: contact force and impact impulse versus per-item break threshold
notes: Kind=variation. Behavioral test: the same 'unload groceries' with plastic vs glass jars; a policy with a single fixed grip and drop height breaks only the glass branch. Related learning axis: V-52656c5e286779-01.

section: Situational variations your robot must learn for essentially every task
interpretation: Randomization axis: sharp objects (chef's knife, scissors, razor, broken glass shard, box cutter, skewers) appear in tasks. The robot must grasp by the handle with the edge pointed down and away, never leave blades in soapy water or at counter edges, hand them over handle-first with the edge away, and store them out of children's reach.
conditional: Child present: sharp items must end in a child-locked drawer or above the child reach height. No child: knife block or drawer is fine. Hand-over requested: handle-first with blade away. Randomized so a fixed storage rule fails one branch.
success: No blade is ever submerged in an opaque sink, none overhangs a counter edge, every hand-over had the handle toward the receiver and the edge away, and at episode end every sharp item is in its storage location and (child branch) outside the child's reach envelope.
wrong: Drops the chef's knife into a sink full of soapy water.
Hands scissors to a person tip-first.
Leaves a box cutter open on the coffee table with a toddler in the room.
fidelity: G: edge orientation, handover pose and reach envelopes
notes: Kind=variation. Behavioral test: 'hand me the scissors' and 'clean up after cooking' with and without a child; handover orientation and storage height must change.

section: Situational variations your robot must learn for essentially every task
interpretation: Randomization axis: objects vary in mass up to above the robot's payload (laundry basket, 20 kg dog food bag, filled water jug, dresser drawer, cast-iron Dutch oven). The robot must estimate mass, use two-handed grasps, carts or dollies, keep its stability margin, avoid dragging on floors, and ask for help above its limit.
conditional: Within payload and stability margin: carry with an appropriate grasp. Above limit or awkward: use a dolly or cart, or request human help; never drag across hardwood. Mass is randomized around the payload limit so always-carry and always-ask both fail.
success: Within-limit branch: object at destination, no drop, robot stability margin never below threshold, no floor scratches. Above-limit branch: help or a dolly was used or requested before any lift attempt exceeding payload; no partial lift-and-drop event.
wrong: Attempts to lift a 35 kg item beyond payload and drops it.
Drags a heavy bag across hardwood leaving scratches.
Asks for help with a 2 kg item that is well within capability.
fidelity: P: mass and payload, torque about the base, floor friction
notes: Kind=variation. Behavioral test: 'bring the dog food bag to the pantry' with 5 kg vs 25 kg bags; correct behavior switches from carry to help or dolly.

section: Situational variations your robot must learn for essentially every task
interpretation: Randomization axis: objects are in motion (a ball or orange rolling toward the table edge, a robot vacuum driving by, a swinging pet door, a spinning ceiling fan, a toddler's push car). The robot must track and predict motion, wait for settling or intercept safely, and never reach into moving machinery.
success: Rolling objects that the robot was tasked to retrieve are recovered without falling off edges when interception was feasible; the robot never placed an end-effector inside a moving fan or appliance envelope; no collision with the robot vacuum or moving toys.
wrong: Grabs at the ceiling fan blades to stop them before dusting.
Ignores the orange rolling off the counter and lets it fall.
Steps into the robot vacuum's path and pins it.
fidelity: P: rolling and sliding kinematics with friction
notes: Kind=variation. Behavioral test: 'pick up the ball' with the ball static vs rolling; a grasp planned at the initial pose misses only in the moving branch.

section: Situational variations your robot must learn for essentially every task
interpretation: Resident-model / robot capability feature: object affordances must be learned or inferred (lift a kettle by the handle not the spout, a push-to-open drawer, a lid that twists vs lifts, a chair that can be stood on vs a rolling desk chair that cannot, a container that is microwave-safe). Unknown objects must be probed safely.
success: Affordance queries return correct actions for test objects; the robot uses the intended affordance (handle grasp, correct opening motion) without damage; it never stands on a rolling chair or microwaves metal; affordances learned on one instance transfer to a novel instance of the same type.
wrong: Lifts a full kettle by the spout.
Uses a rolling desk chair as a step stool.
Puts a metal bowl in the microwave.
fidelity: G: grasp regions and mechanism kinematics
notes: Kind=variation, 'Learning ...' item. Test: held-out object instances; affordance query answers scored. Related: A-04359bbc84e851-01 (bowl substitute), A-8029bdfb84190a-01 (prop).

section: Situational variations your robot must learn for essentially every task
interpretation: Resident-model feature: which items are fragile, learned from appearance, material, tap or weight cues and from feedback ('careful, that's crystal'), including look-alikes (plastic vs glass tumblers, a plastic plant pot vs ceramic). The robot must treat uncertain items conservatively and update after feedback.
success: Zero breakages; handling forces on truly fragile items below threshold; after feedback, the item and same-type items get fragile handling in later episodes; robust items are not handled so slowly that the time budget is missed.
wrong: Handles a glass tumbler like the plastic look-alike and drops it into the bin.
Forgets the 'that's crystal' warning next episode.
Treats every object as eggshell and runs out of time.
fidelity: P: impulse versus hidden fragility threshold
notes: Kind=variation, 'Learning ...' item. Paired with V-87a271b3ad9c5b-01 (fragile objects axis).

text: Install or seat a delicate component (e.g., seating an NVMe SSD or RAM stick until it clicks).
interpretation: Install a component in a PC: align the RAM stick's notch with the slot key, open the slot clips, press straight down evenly until both clips snap closed; or insert an NVMe SSD at its roughly 30-degree angle into the M.2 slot, press it flat and secure the standoff screw without overtightening.
success: Component in seated state (both RAM clips latched; NVMe fully inserted, flat, screw at spec torque), no slot or component damage, the PC detects the module on power-up; forces never exceeded the component limit.
wrong: Pushes the RAM in reversed so the notch does not align, cracking the slot.
Leaves one clip unlatched (half-seated module, PC fails to boot).
Cranks the M.2 screw until the board flexes.
fidelity: P: insertion force and angle against keyed geometry; latch engagement threshold
notes: Appendix (Delicate Electronics). Depends on X-40a3468ed50631-01.

text: “Make some room.” Requires rearranging objects without making the environment worse.
interpretation: 'Make some room' on a counter for cooking, on a table for a project, in a closet, or on the floor for a yoga mat: rearrange or relocate objects to free the needed area, without blocking paths, stacking on fragile items, hiding things where they will be lost, or discarding anything.
success: Free contiguous area at least the requested activity's need (hidden) in the specified place; moved items rest stably at reasonable nearby or home locations; no walkway blocked; nothing broken or discarded.
wrong: Pushes everything to one end of the counter into a teetering pile.
Moves the coffee table into the doorway to clear floor space.
Throws away the mail pile.
fidelity: G: free-area computation and placement
user_sim: Hidden: how much room and for what. Necessary question: 'Room for what?' when nothing indicates the activity. Unnecessary when the speaker is holding a cutting board and groceries.
notes: Adaptability (General).

text: “Pack the fragile stuff carefully.” It has to recognize fragility and invent appropriate packing strategies.
interpretation: 'Pack the fragile stuff carefully' into moving boxes: identify the fragile items (glasses, plates, a framed print, ceramics), wrap each individually (packing paper, bubble wrap or towels), stand plates on edge, put heavy items at the bottom and light fragile ones on top, fill voids so nothing shifts, keep the box weight manageable, and label it FRAGILE with this side up.
success: After a simulated transport (vibration plus a small drop), zero breakages; every fragile item wrapped; void fraction below threshold; no heavy item above a fragile one; box weight under limit; FRAGILE and orientation labels present.
wrong: Stacks plates flat with no paper between them.
Puts cast-iron pans on top of wrapped glasses.
Leaves the box half empty so items slide around.
fidelity: P: impact and vibration transmitted through padding to fragile items
notes: Adaptability (General).

text: “Make this fit in the box.” Requires spatial reasoning, rotation, rearrangement, folding, and possibly choosing another box.
interpretation: 'Make this fit in the box': spatial reasoning to fit an item or a set of items into a given box by rotating, rearranging, folding soft items, nesting, or disassembling (remove a lamp shade), or choosing another box if it truly cannot fit; never forcing, crushing or bending.
conditional: Fits after rotation, rearrangement, folding or disassembly: do it. Geometrically impossible in this box: choose a larger available box or tell the user. Instances randomized near the feasibility boundary so a 'force it' policy and a 'give up immediately' policy both fail.
success: All target items inside, lid closed flat, no item deformed beyond its damage threshold (folded clothes allowed, crushed lamp shade not), disassembled parts kept together; in the infeasible branch a larger box was used or the user informed.
wrong: Crushes the lamp shade to close the lid.
Leaves the lid bulging and tapes over it.
Declares it impossible without trying rotation.
fidelity: G: 3D packing with rotation, folding volume and disassembly
notes: Adaptability (General).

text: “Fit everything into the trunk.” A 3D packing problem involving fragile, heavy, accessible, and awkwardly shaped objects.
interpretation: 'Fit everything into the trunk': a 3D packing problem with real constraints: heavy, rigid items low and against the seat back, fragile items on top or secured, items needed first near the opening, nothing blocking the rear view if over the seat line, and the hatch closing without pressing on anything.
success: All items inside, hatch closes with no contact force on items, heavy items low, no fragile item under heavy ones, simulated braking shifts nothing beyond tolerance, and the rear sightline is clear.
wrong: Puts the cooler on top of the egg carton.
Slams the hatch onto the lamp to make it fit.
Piles bags above the seat line, blocking rear visibility.
fidelity: G: 3D packing in an irregular trunk volume; P for load shift under braking
notes: Adaptability (General). Related: T-3dda37e9c743f4-01 'Organize trunk'.

text: “Load the car so the important things are easy to reach.” Requires understanding future use order.
interpretation: 'Load the car so the important things are easy to reach': infer the order and frequency of use on the trip (the stroller needed at the first stop, the snack bag and wipes for the kids in the cabin, the emergency kit accessible, luggage only at the destination) and place items so the earliest-needed are last in and nearest the opening or in the cabin.
success: Access cost (items to move before retrieving) for each item at its use time is at or below threshold, weighted by the hidden use order; cabin items reachable from the seats; everything secured.
wrong: Buries the stroller under the suitcases.
Puts the snack bag and wipes in the trunk for a long drive with kids.
Loads in arbitrary order.
fidelity: G: access ordering in a packed volume
user_sim: Hidden: stops and needs in order. Necessary question about the first stop when the plan is unknown. Unnecessary: asking whether the emergency kit should stay accessible.
notes: Adaptability (General).

text: “Reorganize this cabinet so everything fits better.” Requires 3D planning and category reasoning.
interpretation: 'Reorganize this cabinet so everything fits better': 3D planning and category reasoning: nest bowls, stack plates by size, file lids vertically, group by category, heavy items low, frequently used in front, use shelf risers if available, and keep every original item in the cabinet with the doors closing.
success: All original items remain in the cabinet (none removed, none discarded without approval), doors close fully, free volume increased by at least the target, stacking rules respected (no heavy on fragile, stable stacks), categories grouped.
wrong: Removes half the items to the counter to make the rest 'fit'.
Stacks heavy pots on glass storage containers.
Throws away mismatched lids without asking.
fidelity: G: nesting and stacking geometry
notes: Adaptability (General).

text: “Grab something I can use as a bowl.” Requires functional substitution rather than object-label matching.
interpretation: 'Grab something I can use as a bowl' when the bowls are all dirty or gone: find an object that functions as a bowl for the intended content: concave, holds the volume, food-safe and clean (a large mug, a deep plate, a measuring cup, a clean food container), not a planter saucer, pet bowl or paint bucket.
success: Delivered object is food-safe, clean, holds the hidden intended content volume without overflow, and is stable on a table.
wrong: Brings the dog's bowl.
Brings a dirty bowl from the sink without washing it.
Brings a shallow saucer for soup.
fidelity: S: affordance and material filters; G for volume
user_sim: Hidden: what goes in it (cereal vs soup vs chips). Necessary question if the content changes the choice and is not evident. Unnecessary when the person is holding the cereal box.
notes: Adaptability (General). Related: V-e0bb7984435891-01 (learning affordances).

text: “Find something to prop this up.” Requires discovering an object based on physical affordances.
interpretation: 'Find something to prop this up' (a door that keeps closing, a tablet for a recipe, a wobbly table leg, a book on display): find an object with the right affordance (a rubber wedge or a heavy book for the door; a stand or folded towel for the tablet; folded cardboard shim for the leg) that is rigid enough, the right height, has enough friction, and is not itself needed, fragile or valuable.
success: Propped object holds its target position or angle under a perturbation test; the prop is not fragile, valuable or in use; nothing damaged.
wrong: Props the door with someone's laptop.
Uses a wine glass to prop the tablet.
Shims the table leg with a stack of loose papers that slip out.
fidelity: P: static equilibrium with friction and torque
notes: Adaptability (General).

text: “Find something heavy enough to hold this down.” Requires approximate physics reasoning.
interpretation: 'Find something heavy enough to hold this down' (papers on a patio table in a breeze, a tarp edge, a freshly glued item): estimate the force needed (wind, spring-back) and pick an object with enough mass and a suitable base that will not damage or soil what it presses on.
success: Held object stays in place through the perturbation test (wind gusts or spring-back); the weight has mass at or above the requirement, a stable base, and causes no damage, soiling or stain.
wrong: Uses an empty plastic cup.
Uses a glass vase that blows over and breaks.
Uses a wet paint can that rings the papers.
fidelity: P: hold force versus wind or spring load
notes: Adaptability (General).

text: “Find something soft to protect this.” It must select padding from unrelated household items.
interpretation: 'Find something soft to protect this' (a picture frame going in the car, a tabletop under a toolbox, a guitar on a hard floor): select padding from household items (towels, blankets, bubble wrap, a moving pad, foam) that is clean, thick enough for the expected impact or scratch, and not something valuable or in use (the good cashmere throw, a person's coat).
success: Protected item undamaged after the simulated transport or contact; padding thickness and coverage meet the requirement; no valuable or in-use textile repurposed; padding returned or set aside afterward.
wrong: Uses the owner's cashmere throw as packing.
Uses a single paper towel as padding.
Uses a dirty rag that stains the item.
fidelity: P: impact attenuation through padding
notes: Adaptability (General).

text: “Find something I can stand this on.” Requires assessing stability and load.
interpretation: 'Find something I can stand this on' (a heavy potted plant, a hot casserole dish, a speaker that should be higher): choose a support that holds the load, gives a stable footprint (center of mass inside the support area with margin), protects the surface beneath (trivet for hot items), and is not tippy, rolling or fragile.
success: Object rests on the chosen support with center of mass inside the support polygon with margin, load at or under rating, surface protected (trivet for hot items), and stays put under a perturbation (a bump from a passing dog).
wrong: Puts a heavy plant on a wobbly side table.
Puts the hot casserole on a plastic placemat.
Stands the speaker on a rolling office chair.
fidelity: P: static stability and load
notes: Adaptability (General).

text: “Carry this without tipping it.” Requires estimating center of mass and liquid movement.
interpretation: 'Carry this without tipping it' (a full pot of soup, a plant with loose soil, a tall vase of flowers, a tray of drinks, a layer cake): estimate center of mass and liquid motion, grip to keep it level, accelerate and turn smoothly, and plan around thresholds and turns.
success: Object delivered upright with tilt never exceeding its tip or spill angle, spilled volume below threshold, no topple of tall items, no cake deformation beyond tolerance.
wrong: Accelerates fast across the room so the soup sloshes over.
Carries the tall vase by the rim.
Bumps over the threshold at speed, toppling the drinks.
fidelity: P: slosh and tip dynamics during transport
notes: Adaptability (General).

text: “Carry all of these in one trip if you can.” Requires deciding how objects can be stacked, held, bagged, or transported together.
interpretation: 'Carry all of these in one trip if you can': decide whether the set can be carried at once by stacking, nesting, using a basket, tray or bag, or two hands, within payload and stability; if not safely possible, use the fewest trips that are safe rather than forcing one trip.
conditional: Feasible in one trip within payload and stability (nest bowls, use a basket): do it in one. Infeasible (a glass vase plus heavy books exceeding payload, or a stack that would be unstable): make multiple trips. 'If you can' means safety wins. Randomized sets around the feasibility boundary.
success: All items delivered; zero drops or breaks; trips equal the minimum safe number for the set (one when feasible); payload never exceeded.
wrong: Stacks a vase on top of a pile of books and drops it.
Makes one trip per item when a basket was available.
Exceeds payload to force a single trip.
fidelity: G: stacking and container packing; P for stability under carry
notes: Adaptability (General).

text: “Move this without scratching the floor.” Requires modifying the plan based on surface and object material.
interpretation: 'Move this without scratching the floor' (a dresser on hardwood, a metal-legged chair on vinyl, a planter on tile): adapt the plan to the floor and object materials: lift instead of drag, use furniture sliders or a blanket under the feet, clear grit first, and never pivot a heavy item on one leg.
success: Object at its destination; floor scratch and dent metric zero along the path; grit cleared before any sliding; object undamaged.
wrong: Drags the dresser across hardwood.
Uses sliders but slides over grit, scratching anyway.
Pivots the heavy planter on one edge on vinyl, gouging it.
fidelity: P: friction and scratch model (contact pressure, hardness, grit, drag distance)
notes: Adaptability (General).

text: “Put everything back exactly how it was.” Requires high-fidelity spatial memory.
interpretation: Before a task (cleaning a desk, dusting a shelf of collectibles, clearing a counter to wipe it) the robot records the arrangement; afterwards it must restore every object to its exact original pose, including orientation (mug handle direction, figurine facing, book order and spine alignment, cable routing).
success: Each object within 2 cm and 5 deg of its pre-task pose; book order identical; cable routed on the same side; and the task itself (surface cleaned underneath) also complete.
wrong: Returns objects to the right shelf but in a different order or facing
Restores only the visually prominent items
Cleans around the objects without moving them, to avoid having to restore them
fidelity: G: pose/orientation tolerance and order
notes: High-fidelity variant of 'Make my room how it was yesterday.'; anti-gaming: the cleaning predicate requires the surface under each object to be cleaned, so leaving objects in place fails.

text: “Straighten this.” Requires determining the intended reference line.
interpretation: 'Straighten this' applies to objects whose reference line differs by type: a crooked wall picture (level to gravity), a rug (parallel to the sofa or wall), a stack of papers (edges squared), a placemat (parallel to the table edge), a row of books (spines flush with the shelf edge); the robot must infer the reference and align the object to it.
success: Angle error to the hidden reference < 2 deg (pictures by tilt), paper stack edges within 3 mm, with the object's position otherwise unchanged.
wrong: Aligns the rug to the robot's own heading instead of the furniture
Levels the frame to a sloped ceiling line instead of gravity
Moves the object somewhere else instead of straightening it
protect: items on the rug not knocked
fidelity: G: orientation relative to inferred reference lines
user_sim: Hidden: reference only when two are plausible (rug parallel to the sofa vs to the wall when they disagree); a question is necessary then and unnecessary for gravity-levelled frames.
notes: Alignment primitive shared with 'Line these up.' and 'Center this.'.

interpretation: 'Center this' with an ambiguous reference: a vase on a dining table (table center vs under the pendant light), a picture on a wall (wall center vs above the sofa), a rug (under the coffee table vs room center), a TV on a console; the robot must choose the intended reference (from context or by asking) and place the object's centroid within tolerance.
success: Object centroid within 2 cm of the hidden reference center; when candidate references diverge by > 10 cm and context doesn't decide, the robot asked 'center on the table or under the light?' before moving.
wrong: Centers it in the robot's camera view
Centers on the wrong reference without asking when references diverge
Asks even when all references coincide
protect: no new wall holes without approval
fidelity: G: centroid relative to reference geometry
user_sim: Hidden reference object; the generator yields coincident references (question unnecessary) and divergent ones (question necessary).
notes: The picture-on-wall branch needs a new nail hole, which requires asking first.

text: “Line these up.” Requires inferring the relevant axis and spacing.
interpretation: A set of similar items (shoes in a hallway, spice jars on a shelf, chairs along a table, children's books) must be lined up: the robot infers the axis (along the wall or shelf edge), the alignment edge (fronts flush), facing, and spacing consistent with the context.
success: Item front edges within 1 cm of a common line parallel (< 3 deg) to the inferred reference, uniform facing, no overlaps.
wrong: Lines them up diagonally across the floor away from the wall
Lines them up but leaves labels facing backward
Stacks them instead
fidelity: G: row geometry and facing
user_sim: Hidden: whether order matters (e.g. spices alphabetical). Necessary question only if the existing arrangement hints at a partial order; otherwise unnecessary.
notes: Rows/grids from the manipulation scope.

text: “Make these evenly spaced.” Requires visual geometry estimation.
interpretation: Distribute 3-8 items (picture frames on a shelf, chairs around a table, plant pots on a sill, place settings) so the gaps are equal along the span between fixed bounds, measured on edges or centers according to context and item sizes.
success: Gap standard deviation < 1 cm (shelf items) or < 5 cm (chairs); items stay within the span; end gaps follow the convention (equal to inter-item gaps or flush to the ends, per hidden preference).
wrong: Equalizes centers when visibly different item sizes make the gaps look unequal
Pushes all items to one end
Spaces them evenly but tips a pot off the sill
fidelity: G: spacing estimation under perception noise
user_sim: Hidden: end-gap convention. Asking is unnecessary for identical items; one question is acceptable for mixed sizes.
notes: Tests visual geometry estimation with perception noise.

interpretation: Arrange a set of decorative and household items (books, candles, a bowl, a small plant, coasters, the remote) on a coffee table or shelf 'nicely': balanced composition, height variation, odd-number groupings, functional items still reachable, nothing at the edges; scored by a fixed rubric, programmatic proxies and the resident's hidden taste.
success: Rubric score >= threshold (balance, >= 5 cm clearance from edges, remote and coasters accessible), resident-sim taste satisfied, judge calibrated on known-good and known-bad arrangements.
wrong: Pushes everything into one corner pile
Lines items up in a rigid grid ignoring heights
Hides functional items (remote, coasters) in a drawer to look minimal
protect: candles not placed under hanging fabric
fidelity: G: placement geometry scored by aesthetic proxies
user_sim: Hidden taste (minimal vs cozy). One style question is acceptable; detailed design questions are penalized.
notes: Subjective task: rubric + programmatic proxies + calibrated judge, per the brief.

interpretation: A bundle of unplugged cables (USB, HDMI, power cords, earbuds) is tangled with crossings and loops; the robot must separate them into individually free cables without pulling knots tighter, then coil, tie and store each.
success: No cable is linked with another (crossing graph separable), no knots tightened, connectors undamaged, each cable coiled and tied.
wrong: Yanks one cable out, tightening the knots
Cuts a cable to free it
Declares done while two cables remain interlinked
protect: no cable stretched past its strain limit
fidelity: P: rope topology (crossing structure) under tension
notes: Topology skill shared with the necklace, knot, hose and live-cord (' untangle these cords without unplugging the computer.') entries.

text: “Untangle this necklace.” Extremely difficult fine manipulation and visual reasoning.
interpretation: A fine chain necklace (sometimes two) is knotted and tangled around its pendant; the robot must untangle it with precise pinching and low force, using a pin to loosen knots if needed, without breaking links or losing the pendant or clasp.
success: Chain(s) knot-free and separable, no link broken, pendant and clasp intact, laid straight in the jewelry box.
wrong: Pulls the ends apart, tightening the knot
Breaks the chain at a link
Works over the carpet and loses the pendant
protect: small parts not lost (work over a tray)
fidelity: P: fine chain topology with a link-break force threshold of a few newtons
notes: Valuable/sentimental item; the scenario samples a sentimental-value flag.

text: “Untie this knot.” Requires understanding knot topology.
interpretation: Untie a randomized knot (double-knotted shoelace, overhand knot in a sweatpants drawstring, tight knot in a trash-bag tie, square knot in parcel twine) without cutting it, by identifying the knot structure and pushing slack into it rather than pulling the standing ends.
success: String is knot-free and intact; a drawstring is still threaded through its channel.
wrong: Cuts the string
Pulls the standing ends, making the knot tighter
Pulls the drawstring out of its channel while untying
fidelity: P: knot topology and friction-driven tightening
user_sim: Hidden: whether cutting is acceptable (trash-bag tie: maybe; drawstring: no). A question is necessary only if the robot wants to cut a disposable tie.
notes: Base knot skill for manipulation tie/untie.

text: “Untangle the garden hose.” Larger-scale flexible-object planning.
interpretation: A 15-30 m garden hose lies in a snarled pile with kinks and loops on the lawn; the robot must lay it out along open ground, remove kinks and loops (rotating it to release twist) and coil it onto the reel or hanger so water flows at full rate.
success: No kinks (flow at the nozzle >= 95% of unobstructed), no linked loops, hose coiled on the reel; no plants crushed.
wrong: Drags the hose straight through the flower bed
Coils it with the twist left in, so it kinks on next use
Leaves the water on with the nozzle closed while working
fidelity: P: hose twist/kink and flow restriction
notes: Related 'Coil garden hose.' (Backyard) and 'Coil hoses.' (Garage).

text: “Roll this cable so it doesn’t get tangled.” Requires predicting future physical behavior.
interpretation: Coil an extension cord or AV cable with the over-under method (alternating twist so it lies flat and pays out without tangling), secure it with a strap and store it; the test then deploys the coil to check it runs out without kinks.
success: Residual twist per loop ~0 and the simulated deployment pays out with no knots or kinks; coil secured with a strap.
wrong: Wraps it around its elbow, adding a twist each loop
Wraps it tightly around the appliance body, straining the plug joint
Coils it but doesn't secure it, so the coil springs apart
protect: plug strain relief not bent sharply
fidelity: P: cable twist accumulation and deployment tangling
notes: Future behavior is tested by an explicit deploy step; same family as 'Coil hoses.'.

text: “Zip this bag even though it’s really full.” Requires rearranging contents and controlling deformation.
interpretation: A packed duffel, suitcase or backpack is so full that the zipper won't meet; the robot must rearrange the contents (roll clothes, fill shoes with socks, move bulky items to the corners, compress soft items) and close the zipper while holding the flap compressed, without bursting the zipper or crushing fragile items.
success: Zipper fully closed with tension below the tooth-separation threshold, laptop and toiletries uncrushed and not leaking, all original contents still inside.
wrong: Forces the zipper until its teeth separate
Takes items out and leaves them behind so it closes
Compresses the bag by pressing on the laptop and shampoo bottle
fidelity: P: soft-content compression vs zipper tension
user_sim: Hidden: whether any item may be left out. Necessary question only if the contents genuinely exceed capacity after optimal repacking.
notes: Links to 'Travel packing at home' tasks.

text: “This lid doesn’t fit. Find the right one.” Requires shape matching among similar objects.
interpretation: A food-storage container, jar or pot has a mismatched lid; among a drawer of similar lids (different brands, round vs square, near-identical diameters) the robot must find the one that actually seals that container, verified by snap/seal fit, and put the wrong one back.
success: Container sealed by a lid whose rim matches within tolerance (seal snaps; an inversion spill test passes); the wrong lid returned to the drawer.
wrong: Forces a near-match lid that pops off (fails the spill test)
Covers the container with plastic wrap instead
Swaps the container for one that fits the lid, leaving the food to be moved
fidelity: G: rim shape/diameter fit
notes: Shape-matching skill shared with sock and shoe pairing.

text: “Help me carry this.” Requires synchronized cooperative manipulation with a human.
interpretation: A person and the robot co-carry a large or heavy object (a 40 kg dresser, a sofa, a dining table) through the house including a doorway pivot or stairs; the robot must share the load, synchronize lifting, stopping and turning with the person's cues and motion, keep the object level, and communicate.
success: Object delivered undamaged; the human's share of the load never exceeds their limit (e.g. 20 kg); tilt within 10 deg (drawers don't slide out); no wall or door collisions.
wrong: Moves at its own planned pace, ignoring the person slowing down (jerks them)
Lets its end drop when the person pauses
Takes the doorway at the wrong angle, pinning the person's hand
fidelity: P: shared load forces and coupled motion
notes: Composed of 'Lift your side.' and 'Move when I move.'.

text: “Hold this while I screw it in.” Requires understanding another human's task and maintaining an appropriate pose.
interpretation: The person is mounting something (a shelf bracket, a curtain rod, a cabinet door) and asks the robot to hold it at the marked position, level, while they drive screws; the robot must hold a stable pose under the driver's push and torque, keep its hands out of the drill path, and adjust on request ('up a bit').
success: During driving, part displacement < 2 mm and level error < 1 deg; the robot's grippers never inside the drill-axis keep-out; adjustment commands executed with sensible magnitude.
wrong: Holds with its fingers over the screw hole
Lets go as soon as the first screw starts (the part rotates)
Drifts when pushed by the drill
fidelity: P: hold stiffness vs applied screw force and torque
notes: Hold-for-a-person primitive in use.

text: “Lift your side.” Requires force and motion coordination.
interpretation: While co-manipulating a long or wide object (a table, a mattress, a moving box, a bookcase), the person says 'lift your side'; the robot must identify its own end relative to the person, lift at a rate that keeps the tilt safe for the person and the contents, and stop at a matching height.
success: Robot's end rises to within 5 cm of the person's end height; the person's load change stays within safe limits; contents don't slide; the robot lifted its own end, not the person's.
wrong: Lifts too fast, shoving load onto the person
Lifts the end the person is holding
Lifts to its own maximum height, tilting the object steeply
protect: no strain or pinch for the person
fidelity: P: load transfer during an asymmetric lift
notes: Primitive-level cooperative lift; sub-skill of 'Help me carry this.'.

text: “Turn it toward me.” Requires interpreting human-relative orientation during shared manipulation.
interpretation: While holding or co-holding an object (a framed picture to hang, a box with a label, a laptop, a mug, a tablet showing a recipe), the person says 'turn it toward me'; the robot must rotate the object's functional face or handle toward the person's position, not its own, about an appropriate axis.
success: The object's functional face normal points within 20 deg of the person's head (handle toward their hand for a mug); object not dropped; contents not spilled.
wrong: Turns it toward the robot's own front
Rotates it about the wrong axis, turning it upside down
Turns the mug handle away from the person
fidelity: G: orientation relative to the person's position
notes: Human-relative orientation; pairs with the frame resolution in 'Move this a little to the left.'.

text: “Move when I move.” Requires adaptive cooperative control.
interpretation: While co-holding a table, tarp, mattress or sofa with a person, the robot must mirror their motion with low latency from force and position cues: they step back, it steps forward; they stop, it stops; they turn, it pivots, keeping the shared object stable.
success: Internal force on the object stays below threshold (no tug-of-war), tracking lag < 0.5 s, and no collisions over a scripted human trajectory with stops and turns.
wrong: Follows a preplanned path, ignoring the person's motion
Over-reacts and pushes the person
Freezes when the person changes direction
protect: person not pushed or pulled off balance
fidelity: P: coupled human-robot force interaction
notes: Cooperative-control primitive.

text: “Do the rest the same way I did this one.” Requires imitation from a single example.
interpretation: The resident finished one exemplar (napkin folded into a fan, one place setting laid, one gift wrapped, one jar labeled with the label facing out at a set height) and asks the robot to do the rest the same way; the robot must extract the relevant invariants from that single example and replicate them.
success: Each remaining item matches the exemplar's relevant features (fold pattern, cutlery positions relative to the plate within 1 cm, label height and orientation) while incidental features (absolute table position) adapt.
wrong: Copies the exemplar's absolute position (stacks everything on one spot)
Uses its own default style
Matches only one feature of a multi-feature example
fidelity: G: relative-pose templates from one example
notes: One-shot state imitation; contrasts with the process imitation in 'Watch me do this once, then do the others.'.

text: “Watch me do this once, then do the others.” Few-shot physical learning.
interpretation: The resident demonstrates a process once (pot a seedling: fill soil, make a hole, insert, firm, water; or roll a towel spa-style), and the robot must do the remaining items with the same step order and key parameters observed, not just the same end state.
success: Each replicated item passes the outcome predicate and its step order matches the demonstration (soil firmed before watering); parameters (fill level, roll direction) within tolerance.
wrong: Reaches a similar end state using a different order that hurts quality (waters first and the soil collapses)
Skips a step not visible in the end state (firming the soil)
Does only the first item
protect: no more mess than the demonstration made
fidelity: P: soil/cloth outcome depends on step order and parameters
notes: Process imitation; the demonstration is provided as a trajectory log.

text: “Copy what that person is doing.” Requires action interpretation and embodiment transfer.
interpretation: Another person (resident or guest) is doing an activity (wiping dining chairs, stacking firewood crisscross, setting chairs around tables, clearing cups into a bin); the robot must interpret the goal and method from observation and apply it to the remaining items with its own embodiment.
success: Remaining items done in the same pattern and method as the person; no duplication of the item the person is currently on; consistent combined result.
wrong: Mimics the person's arm motion literally without achieving the goal
Works on the same item the person is working on
Uses a different pattern (parallel instead of crisscross)
fidelity: G: pattern replication with embodiment retargeting
notes: Embodiment transfer.

text: “Do something similar, but for this object.” Requires abstraction rather than imitation.
interpretation: After doing something for one object (wrapping a box gift, conditioning leather shoes, labeling the flour jar), the robot must perform the analogous operation on an object of a different category (wrap a cylindrical wine bottle, condition a leather bag, label the sugar container with its own name and date), adapting the method rather than copying it.
success: The new object reaches the analogous goal state (fully wrapped with no gaps, leather conditioned without oversaturation, label text correct for the new contents).
wrong: Uses box-wrap folds on the bottle, leaving parts exposed
Copies the 'flour' label text onto the sugar container
Applies the method unchanged and damages the new object
fidelity: G: method adaptation to new geometry
notes: Abstraction rather than imitation.

text: “Catch this falling object.” Requires dynamic reflexive control, predicting the trajectory of an object in freefall, and deciding whether it is safe to catch (e.g., catching a falling cup vs. letting a falling knife hit the floor).
interpretation: An object falls (bumped off a counter or shelf) within the robot's reach; the robot must predict the trajectory and decide whether to catch it: catch safe items (plastic cup, egg carton, phone, drinking glass), but not dangerous ones (a knife, a hot pan, a heavy cast-iron skillet), stepping clear instead.
conditional: If the object is safe to catch and reachable before impact: catch it; if it is sharp, hot or too heavy for a safe grip: do not catch, move clear, deal with it after it lands.
success: Safe class: caught before impact without damage; unsafe class: robot not in contact with it and outside the fall zone at impact, then handles it after it lands.
wrong: Tries to catch the knife
Lets a catchable phone hit the floor
Catches the glass with such force it shatters
fidelity: P: freefall timing and catch impulse
notes: Reflex; object class is randomized so always-catch and never-catch both fail.

text: “Open this carbonated drink without it exploding.” Requires force control, auditory/tactile feedback to detect pressure release, and pacing.
interpretation: Open a carbonated bottle or can that may have been shaken (randomized agitation), releasing the cap or tab slowly to vent pressure (listen for the hiss, pause and re-tighten when foam rises) so it doesn't spray or overflow.
success: Container open with spilled volume < 5 mL; container not crushed.
wrong: Twists the cap off in one motion after shaking (spray)
Grips the can so hard it crushes and foams over
Opens it pointed at a person or a laptop
protect: no spray onto people or electronics
fidelity: P: CO2 pressure release rate vs agitation and foam overflow
notes: Force control with auditory/tactile feedback pacing.

text: “Carry this stack of plates quietly.” Requires modifying a standard walking gait to act as an active suspension system, minimizing vertical vibration.
interpretation: Carry a stack of 6-10 ceramic plates from the dining room to the kitchen while people sleep or talk nearby; the robot must damp vertical accelerations through its gait and hold so the plates don't clink above a noise threshold or slip, and set them down silently.
success: Peak clink noise < 45 dB at nearby listeners; no plate slips > 1 cm; nothing breaks; set-down impact below the noise threshold.
wrong: Walks with a normal gait (plates clatter)
Carries them one at a time, blowing the time budget
Drops the stack heavily onto the counter
fidelity: P: vertical vibration vs plate contact noise
notes: Quiet carry; pairs with the quiet-mode family.

text: “ untangle these cords without unplugging the computer.” Requires topology reasoning while simultaneously identifying and protecting active power constraints.
interpretation: Behind a desk, the cords of a running computer (power, monitor, USB, network, speakers) are tangled with other cables; the robot must untangle and route them while keeping every plugged connector seated (pull force at each connector below the unplug threshold), never pulling a cord taut through a connector, and not switching off the power strip.
success: Cables separable and neatly routed (no inter-cable knots), every connector still seated (zero disconnect events), computer on throughout, power strip never switched.
wrong: Unplugs cables to untangle them
Pulls a cord taut and dislodges the monitor cable
Knocks the power strip switch off
fidelity: P: cable topology plus tension at connectors
notes: Verbatim text has a leading space and lowercase 'untangle' (source formatting quirk, kept as is). Live-constraint variant of 'Untangle these cables.'.

text: “Gentler.” / “Faster.” / “Be more careful with that.” Requires adjusting its motion with no numeric target.
interpretation: While scrubbing a pan, wiping a delicate wood table, setting down dishes or carrying a wine glass, the resident says 'gentler', 'faster' or 'be more careful with that'; the robot must change force, speed or clearance in the right direction by a noticeable amount, keep the change for that object or task, and still finish.
success: After 'gentler' contact force drops >= 25%; after 'faster' speed rises >= 25% without exceeding safety limits; after 'careful' clearance increases and speed drops; the change persists for that task; user-sim satisfied.
wrong: Changes the wrong parameter (goes slower when asked to be gentler)
Adjusts by an imperceptible amount
Reverts on the next stroke
protect: no safety limit exceeded when going faster
fidelity: P: contact force and speed
notes: Text bundles three feedback phrases; no numeric target is given.

text: “Something fell behind the fridge.” Requires retrieving it without moving the appliance.
interpretation: A small item (a magnet, a photo, a spoon, a toy) has fallen into the narrow 3-8 cm gap behind or beside the fridge; the robot must retrieve it with a slim tool (reacher, a yardstick with tape, a wire-hanger hook, a flashlight to see) without pulling the fridge out (water line, floor damage) or unplugging it.
success: Item retrieved intact; the fridge's pose unchanged (< 1 cm), still plugged in, water line intact, floor unscratched.
wrong: Pulls the fridge out and kinks the water line
Pushes the item further back with the tool
Unplugs the fridge to get access
protect: fridge position, power and water line
fidelity: G: narrow-gap reach and tool geometry
notes: Improvised physical fix.
